question: What is preregistration and why is it important?
answer:
**Preregistration** is the practice of publicly documenting the research plan — including hypotheses, analysis code, and the criteria that will determine whether a replication is deemed successful — *before* any data are examined. In the handbook this is described as “a description of the planned study or analysis prior to their execution” that “specifies the planned study or analysis prior to their execution” and “prevents unintended flexibility in how the data are analyzed”[2]. For replication work, the preregistration should also spell out the success criteria and an analysis plan (ideally with tested code) so that the replication can be evaluated transparently[1].  

**Why it matters**

- **Reduces questionable research practices.**  A preregistration (and a pre‑analysis plan) dramatically cuts researchers’ “degrees of freedom,” limiting p‑hacking and “null hacking” and thereby lowering publication bias[2].  Empirical evidence shows that preregistration and pre‑analysis plans reduce p‑hacking and publication bias in large samples of test statistics[1].  
- **Increases transparency and credibility.**  By stating hypotheses and analysis decisions up‑front, reviewers and readers can see exactly what was planned versus what was done, making any deviations easy to spot and justify[1].  
- **Facilitates Registered Reports.**  When a preregistration is submitted as a Registered Report, the methods are peer‑reviewed and accepted before data collection, so the eventual publication decision no longer depends on the results, further protecting against bias[1].  

**How to preregister**

- Use existing templates (e.g., the Brandt et al. 2014 template) or OSF‑based templates such as [https://osf.io/7xrn9](https://osf.io/7xrn9) and [https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home](https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home)[1].  
- Submit the preregistration to a journal that offers Registered Reports or to a platform like [Peer Community in Registered Reports (PCI‑RR)](https://rr.peercommunityin.org)[1]

question: How do I preregister my longitudinal research?
answer:
**Preregistering a longitudinal study**  

1. **What preregistration means** – It is a “dissertation‑proposal‑style” document where you lay out every part of the study before you collect data, so that reviewers and future readers can see exactly what you planned [1].  

2. **Key elements to include**  
   * **Research questions / hypotheses** – state the substantive predictions for each wave of data.  
   * **Design details** – describe the number of measurement occasions, the interval between them, the instruments or interview protocols you will use, and any sampling or recruitment plans.  
   * **Participant information & positionality** – note who will take part and, for qualitative work, your own background and how it may influence the study [1].  
   * **Analysis plan** – specify the statistical or coding procedures you will apply to the longitudinal data (e.g., growth‑curve modelling, repeated‑measures ANOVA, thematic analysis across time).  
   * **Success criteria** – define in advance what outcomes would count as a successful replication of your hypotheses (e.g., effect‑size thresholds, model‑fit indices) [2].  
   * **Ethics & data‑sharing plan** – outline consent procedures, how you will protect participant confidentiality, and what materials (e.g., interview guides, codebooks) you intend to make openly available [1].  

3. **Choose a preregistration template** – The replication handbook points to a standard template by Brandt et al. (2014) and to two OSF collections of templates that work for many study types, including longitudinal designs [2]:  

   * <https://osf.io/7xrn9>  
   * <https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home>  

4. **Where to host the preregistration** – Upload the completed document to a time‑stamped, open‑access repository such as the Open Science Framework (OSF). The OSF link above will let you create a project, attach your preregistration file, and obtain a permanent DOI.

question: How do I preregister qualitative research?
answer:
To preregister a qualitative study, treat the preregistration like a detailed dissertation‑proposal that you post **before** you begin data collection. In the preregistration you should lay out:

* Who the researchers are and their positionality.  
* The study context, research questions, theoretical framework, sampling strategy, interview or observation procedures, and the planned analysis approach. This level of detail lets others see exactly how you intend to conduct the work and prevents later changes to the methods [1].

You can submit this plan to a preregistration platform (e.g., the Center for Open Science) or as a **registered report** with a journal that offers a publication agreement [1]. Doing so creates a public record of your intended methods, supporting transparency and rigor in qualitative research.  

For more information on the community that discussed these practices, see the [Virtual Unconference on Open Scholarship Practices in Education Research](https://www.cos.io/education-reseach-2021-virtual-unconference#:~:text=February%208%2D9%2C%202021&text=The%20unconference%20included%20engaging%20plenary,detailed%20guidance%20for%20education%20researchers) sponsored by the [Center for Open Science](https://www.cos.io/) [1].

question: Where can I preregister my research?
answer:
You can preregister your study on any open‑science platform that supports a preregistration template. The replication handbook points to the Open Science Framework (OSF) as a common place to find ready‑made templates [2] and provides two direct links:

* OSF preregistration template collection <https://osf.io/7xrn9> [2]  
* Additional OSF templates <https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home> [2]

If you want your preregistration to be reviewed as part of a **Registered Report**, you can submit the plan to a journal that offers this format (a list of such journals is available [2]) or use the community‑run platform **Peer Community in Registered Reports (PCI‑RR)**, which reviews pre‑prints and then forwards accepted papers to participating journals <https://rr.peercommunityin.org> [2].

In short, the OSF sites are the primary places to upload a preregistration, and you can also link it to a Registered Report via journal portals or PCI‑RR.

question: How is preregistration different from registered report?
answer:
Preregistration is the act of publicly posting a detailed plan for a study **before any data are collected**. It specifies the hypotheses, the analysis plan (often with code), and, for replications, explicit success criteria that define what would count as a successful or failed replication [1]. A preregistration alone does not involve any formal peer review of the methods; it simply creates a time‑stamped record that can be checked later to guard against p‑hacking and undisclosed analytic flexibility [1].

A Registered Report (sometimes called a Registered Replication Report) goes a step further: the preregistration is submitted to a journal **and undergoes peer review** before data collection begins. If the reviewers and editors are satisfied with the proposed methods, the manuscript is **accepted in principle** for publication, and the eventual decision to publish does not depend on the nature of the results [1]. This format therefore reduces publication bias toward “positive” findings and is especially valuable for replications, which often produce null or inconclusive outcomes [1].

In practice, a Registered Report includes a preregistration as its core component, but it is embedded in a journal‑based review process and results in an “in‑principle acceptance” that a plain preregistration does not provide [1].

**Useful resources**

- A specific preregistration template (Brandt et al., 2014) and other templates are listed at [https://osf.io/7xrn9](https://osf.io/7xrn9) and [https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home](https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home) [1].  
- A spreadsheet of journals that offer Registered Reports (not limited to replications) is available [here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0) [1].  
- The Peer Community in Registered Reports platform for reviewing pre‑prints is [https://rr.peercommunityin.org](https://rr.peercommunityin.org) [1].

question: Will people find my preregistration?
answer:
Yes—if you make your preregistration publicly available, other researchers can easily find it. The handbook recommends posting the preregistration on an open platform (e.g., OSF) and using one of the available templates [1]. You can also submit the study as a Registered Report, which requires the preregistration to be peer‑reviewed and posted before data collection [1].  

**How to ensure visibility**

* **Upload to OSF** – the handbook points to two OSF locations that host preregistration templates and examples:  
  * <https://osf.io/7xrn9> [1]  
  * <https://osf.io/zab38/wiki/home> [1]  

* **Registered Reports** – many journals accept Registered Reports; a spreadsheet of such journals is available online [1].  

* **Peer Community in Registered Reports (PCI‑RR)** – you can post your preregistration on the PCI‑RR platform, where the pre‑print is reviewed and then can be linked to participating journals [1].  

* **Version‑history uploads** – most preregistration platforms (including OSF) let you upload amendments with a preserved version history, so any changes remain transparent [1].  

By posting your preregistration on one of these open repositories (or as part of a Registered Report/PCI‑RR submission), it will be searchable and discoverable by anyone interested in your replication.

question: What is open access and what are advantages and disadvantages?
answer:
**Open access** is the practice of making research outputs—such as publications, data, code, and other research products—freely available to anyone who wishes to read, use, or reuse them, while still respecting cultural diversity, security, and privacy [3].

### Advantages of open access
- **Broader reach of knowledge** – By removing paywalls, open access increases the amount of knowledge that can be accessed by anyone, expanding opportunities for participation in science [3].
- **Greater inclusivity and equity** – Open access helps include researchers and audiences from diverse backgrounds and varying levels of training, fostering a more equitable research community [3].
- **Enhanced transparency and reproducibility** – When research results are openly available, they can be more easily examined, replicated, and built upon, leading to more reliable and trustworthy science [3].
- **Facilitates collaboration** – Free access to research products encourages collaboration across institutions, disciplines, and countries [3].
- **Supports open‑access publishing education** – The Open Research Toolkit includes a dedicated module on “Open Access to Published Research,” providing ready‑to‑use slide decks, videos, and notes for teaching these concepts [1].

### Disadvantages / challenges of open access
- **Resource and training needs** – Implementing open‑access practices often requires additional resources, infrastructure, and educator training, which many institutions currently lack [2].
- **Balancing openness with security and privacy** – Open access must be managed in a way that respects security, privacy, and cultural considerations, which can complicate the sharing of certain data or methods [3].
- **Potential costs for authors** – Some open‑access publishing models shift costs to authors (e.g., article‑processing charges), which can be a financial barrier for some researchers [1] (the toolkit notes the need for “more resources and training for educators” as a challenge

question: How can I make sure nobody misuses my openly available data?
answer:
To protect openly‑available data from misuse, the Open Research Toolkit recommends the following steps:

1. **Choose a clear, permissive license** – Assign a Creative Commons 4.0 Attribution (CC‑By) license to all original data and software. This lets anyone reuse the material **as long as they give you proper credit**, and it makes the reuse terms explicit from the start[1].  

2. **Document licensing and usage expectations** – Include the license statement and any specific conditions (e.g., “no commercial use” or “share‑alike”) in the data’s metadata, README files, and any repository landing pages. The “Open Licensing of Data & Software” module provides templates and examples you can adopt[1].  

3. **Apply FAIR principles** – Make the data **Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable** with clear provenance information. FAIR documentation helps users understand how the data should be handled and cited, reducing accidental misuse[1].  

4. **Provide attribution guidance** – Supply a citation format or a suggested acknowledgment text so that downstream users know exactly how to credit you. This reinforces proper use and makes any deviation easier to spot.  

5. **Monitor adoption** – The toolkit’s author asks users to report how they use the material, which can help you track who is reusing your data and whether it’s being applied appropriately[1].  

6. **Offer a point of contact** – List an email address for questions or concerns about data use. The toolkit’s contact information is OpenResearch@utk.edu or ceaker@utk.edu[1].

question: What are the best platforms and tools for sharing research data openly?
answer:
Here are some of the most widely‑used platforms and tools that the FORRT community highlights for openly sharing research data:

- **Domain‑specific repositories** – RCSB Protein Data Bank for structural biology (https://www.rcsb.org/), ChemRxiv for chemistry preprints and data (https://chemrxiv.org/), ECSarXiv for earth‑science data (https://ecsarxiv.org), PhysioNet for physiological signals (https://physionet.org/), and the International Brain Laboratory data portal (https://www.internationalbrainlab.com/) for neuroscience [1].

question: What are the legal and ethical considerations in sharing human subject data?
answer:
Legal and ethical considerations for sharing human‑subject data revolve around protecting participants’ privacy, respecting consent, and complying with institutional and regulatory rules.

* **Informed consent and IRB approval** – Any plan to share interview protocols, coding notebooks, or raw data must be built into the consent form and approved by the Institutional Review Board. This ensures that participants are aware of who may access the data and that the sharing does not breach ethical boundaries [1].  
* **Privacy and confidentiality** – Qualitative data often contain detailed, potentially identifying information. Researchers must evaluate how much detail can be released without risking re‑identification of participants, especially when large amounts of data are involved [1].  
* **Legal restrictions** – Even when researchers wish to be fully open, they may be limited by “ethical and legal limitations” that prevent sharing certain materials. When sharing is permissible, it should be done under an open license that respects any remaining constraints [3].  
* **Data‑management ethics** – Resources on “ethics specific to data management” (e.g., secure storage, controlled access, de‑identification procedures) are recommended to guide responsible sharing [1].  

Together, these points highlight that open‑science practices for human‑subject data must balance transparency with the duty to protect participants, requiring clear consent, IRB oversight, careful de‑identification, and adherence to any applicable legal or institutional policies.  

**Helpful resources**

* COREQ guidelines for reporting researcher background and study details [1](https://academic.oup.com/view-large/27217733)  
* Open Educational Resources list of tools and publications [1](https://www.oercommons.org/courseware/lesson/80058)  
* FORRT Replication Database for submitting replication results under appropriate licensing [3](https://t1p.de/fred_submit)

question: How does open science reshape the future of interdisciplinary and collaborative research?
answer:
Open science is defined as “the principle and practice of making research products and processes available to all… fostering collaborations, reproducibility, and equity” [3]. By opening every stage of the research cycle—from idea generation to data sharing—open science creates the technical and cultural infrastructure that makes interdisciplinary teamwork possible.

**Shared platforms turn isolated labs into global teams.**  
Projects such as the **Many Babies** collaboration involve 69 laboratories in 16 countries, using a common protocol, openly shared materials on GitHub and the Open Science Framework (OSF) [2]. The **PLAY** project similarly makes all home‑visit protocols, video, and questionnaire data freely downloadable [2]. **Open‑science resources connect diverse disciplines.**

question: What should you think about when sharing your data with others?
answer:
When you share your data with others, you should keep the following points in mind:

* **Legal and ethical constraints** – Only share data that you are allowed to share. Respect any privacy, confidentiality, or copyright restrictions that may apply, and be aware of the ethical and legal limitations of the dataset [1].

* **Open licensing** – If possible, release the data under an open licence so that others can reuse it freely. This is part of the best‑practice transparency and openness promotion guidelines (TOP) [1].

* **Full documentation** – Provide a link to the preregistration, analysis plan, and analysis script, and include clear metadata or a codebook that describes all variables. Comprehensive documentation makes the data understandable and reusable [1].

* **Transparency of the research process** – Share all materials (e.g., questionnaires, code) together with the data so that the entire workflow can be reproduced [1].

* **Consider the context of the original work** – Recognise that older studies may have been collected under different norms (e.g., data sharing was less common in the 1990s). Explain any limitations that stem from the historical context [1].

* **Use the FORRT Replication Database** – You can enter your data and results through the guided survey, which makes the findings visible to the community [1][https://t1p.de/fred_submit](https://t1p.de/fred_submit).

These considerations align with the broader open‑science definition, which emphasizes making research products available while respecting security, privacy, and diverse cultural contexts [2].

question: How do you update your knowledge base, and are these updates made transparent?
answer:
FORRT keeps its knowledge base current by publishing new content, code, and data on its public website and in open‑source repositories, and by announcing every change through release notes and regular communications.  

* **Release‑note updates** – The Flora Validator page shows a “What’s new” section that lists every change since the last visit, making each update visible to users [3].  
* **Open‑source code** – The ELD CAMA platform’s underlying code is hosted on GitHub, where every commit and new version is publicly recorded [1].  
* **Project‑wide announcements** – New features, data‑curation opportunities and other developments are highlighted in the FORRT newsletter and on the online FORRT calendar, which are freely accessible to the community [2].  

All of these mechanisms are openly displayed, so anyone can see what has been added or modified and when.  

**Useful links**  

* Flora Validator release notes – <https://forrt.org/flora-validation/> [3]  
* ELD CAMA source repository – <https://github.com/metahag/ELD-CAMA_source> [1]  
* FORRT calendar of events – <https://forrt.org/about/get-involved/#calendar> [2]

question: What is transparency?
answer: Transparency is a core principle of open research that means making the details of a study—its data, methods, analysis, and reporting—open, clear, and accessible so that others can understand, evaluate, and reproduce the work [1]. In practice, it is expressed through standards and tools (such as the Transparency Checklist) that teach and ensure research reports are credible, fully documented, and openly shared [3].

question: How do licensing agreements affect the sharing and reuse of scientific research?
answer:
Licensing agreements are the key mechanism that determines how freely scientific outputs can be shared, reused, and adapted.

**Open licenses enable unrestricted sharing and reuse**  
- The handbook advises that replication data, materials, and analysis scripts should be shared “under an open license” so that anyone can access and reuse them, subject only to attribution requirements [1].  
- The Open Research Toolkit explicitly uses a Creative Commons 4.0 Attribution (CC‑BY) license for all its original content, which “anyone can use and adapt however they like with attribution to the author” [3][<https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/>].  

**Institutional recommendations reinforce open licensing**  
- Many institutions and libraries suggest adding a CC‑BY disclaimer to journal submissions, giving researchers the right to reuse the accepted manuscript freely [1].  
- Choosing “diamond Open Access” journals (no publishing or reading fees) is encouraged for maximal openness, whereas “gold OA” journals often require article processing charges (APCs) [1].

question: What ethical concerns arise in the context of increased transparency and openness in research?
answer:
Increasing transparency and openness in research raises several ethical concerns.

* **Participant privacy and identifiability** – Sharing open materials such as interview protocols, coding notebooks, or raw data can create audit trails that make it possible to re‑identify participants, especially when qualitative data contain sensitive information. Researchers must therefore plan how to protect identities and obtain explicit consent for any sharing, following IRB and ethical guidelines [2].

* **Informed consent and IRB compliance** – Any decision to make materials or data publicly available must be incorporated into the study’s consent procedures and approved by an Institutional Review Board, ensuring that participants are aware of how their information may be used and that ethical boundaries are not violated [2].

* **Potential harm to minoritized scholars** – More open peer‑review models (e.g., disclosed reviewer identities or public reviews) can expose reviewers and authors to backlash, harassment, or negative career consequences, particularly for those from historically excluded groups. This raises equity and safety concerns that must be considered when designing open‑review systems [1].

* **Power imbalances and inequitable participation** – Openness may inadvertently favor scholars with more power or majority identities, while those in less powerful positions may feel pressured to stay silent or may experience increased scrutiny, leading to ethical questions about fairness and inclusion in open‑science practices [1].

* **Balancing transparency with ethical responsibility** – While transparent reporting (e.g., detailed methodological descriptions, preregistration) improves rigor, researchers must weigh the benefits against the risk of exposing vulnerable participants or contributors, ensuring that openness does not compromise ethical standards [2].

**Resources for ethical guidance**

* COREQ guidelines for transparency about researchers and their background

question: How is citizen science open science?
answer:
Citizen science is a concrete expression of open‑science principles. Open science is defined as “the principle and practice of making research products and processes available to all… fostering collaborations, reproducibility, and equity” [1]. Citizen science puts this into practice by treating members of the public as active contributors to knowledge production—students and participants help design, conduct, and share research, which mirrors the open‑science emphasis on transparency, shared data, and inclusive collaboration [3]. In the FORRT teaching‑open‑science program, citizen science is listed under the “participatory lens” module, which focuses on “students and participants as active members of knowledge production” [3]. Thus, citizen science embodies open science by opening the research process to broader participation, encouraging reproducible methods, and expanding access to scientific results.

- Open‑science definition: <https://open.science.gov/> [1]  
- FORRT “Teaching Open Science” page (see Module 2 description): <https://forrt.org/teaching_os/> [3]

question: What are the key skills needed for career advancement in academia?
answer:
**Key skills that help you move forward in an academic career**

- **Publishing – producing high‑quality research papers** – Academic hiring is driven mainly by the *quantity and quality of your publications* rather than grades or transcripts [1].
- **Research design and project‑management expertise** – A PhD gives you transferable skills in planning studies, managing long‑term projects, and overseeing data collection [1].
- **Writing proficiency** – Regular, disciplined writing (papers, reports, thesis chapters) makes the writing process easier and improves the quality of your outputs [1].
- **Presentation and public‑speaking ability** – Giving talks, guest lectures, and conference presentations builds a skill that is *valued inside and outside of academia* [1].
- **Networking** – Making connections at conferences, during poster sessions, and through informal meetings is often the most important factor for career opportunities [1].
- **Technical up‑skilling (coding, statistics, data tools)** – Learning programming languages, statistical methods, and data‑visualisation tools (e.g., R, SQL, PowerBi, Tableau) expands the range of research you can do and makes you more competitive [1][3].
- **Teaching and mentorship** – Experience in teaching, supervising students, and mentoring peers is a core academic competency [1].
- **Self‑discipline and flexibility** – Managing an unstructured schedule, staying motivated without strict deadlines, and adapting to different work environments are essential for success [1].
- **Supervisor‑relationship management** – Knowing how to communicate effectively with your supervisor (e.g., preferred email style, meeting frequency) helps you get the guidance you need [1].

question: How are emerging technologies transforming traditional classroom teaching?
answer:
Emerging digital tools are reshaping classroom teaching by making open‑science resources instantly shareable, interactive and reusable.  Video platforms such as the Center for Open Science channel, the RIOT Science Club, and the “Professor Writes a Scientific Paper in a Day” video let educators embed short, captioned tutorials directly into lectures, while the OSF repository (e.g., [Julia Strand’s course materials](https://osf.io/zpb8a/)) provides a permanent, citable home for syllabi, slides and scripts that students can explore at any time [1][2].  

Open‑educational‑resource (OER) collections (e.g., [LibreTexts](https://libretexts.org/), [OpenStax](https://openstax.org/), [Open Textbook Library](https://open.umn.edu/opentextbooks/)) and federated search tools such as the Mason OER Metafinder let instructors quickly locate and adopt high‑quality textbooks and teaching assets, reducing the time spent creating new content [1].  By publishing these materials under FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) [1], teachers ensure that all learners—including those with disabilities or limited internet bandwidth—can access transcripts, audio versions and multilingual translations.  

Community‑driven platforms further amplify the impact of technology.  ReproducibiliTea journal clubs, the RIOT Science Club, and FORRT’s own Pedagogies hub gather educators worldwide to share videos, slide decks and best‑practice notes, fostering a collaborative culture that continuously updates curricula with the latest open‑science methods [3].  These emerging technologies thus turn the traditional lecture into a dynamic, open, and inclusive learning environment.

question: What are the best practices for managing a successful laboratory and effective team?
answer:
**Best‑practice recommendations for running a thriving laboratory and an effective research team**

- **Rotate the focus of weekly group meetings** – alternate between standard journal discussions, equity/diversity/inclusion (EDI) article reviews, “Slide Improv” sessions, and “Fact or Fiction” critical‑thinking exercises. This keeps meetings fresh, builds diverse skills, and visibly signals the importance of EDI to the group[1].  
- **Use “Slide Improv” to develop on‑the‑spot presentation confidence** – have a student prepare a short five‑slide talk on a topic outside the lab’s core research, then deliver it without animations. Repeated practice reduces fear of “screwing up” and improves overall presenting ability[1].  
- **Incorporate “Fact or Fiction” for critical‑thinking training** – ask a student to present brief summaries of three papers, one of which is fabricated, and let the group identify the fake. This fun activity sharpens analytical skills[1].  
- **Conduct an annual anonymous lab‑climate poll** – use a short Google Form to ask about quality of life, what works well, and what needs improvement. The results help pinpoint hidden issues and celebrate strengths[1].

question: Hoe kan ik kwalitatief onderzoek preregistreren?
answer:
Om kwalitatief onderzoek te preregistreren kun je de volgende stappen volgen:

1. **Schrijf een gedetailleerd onderzoeksplan**  
   Leg je onderzoeksvraag, theoretisch kader, steekproefstrategie, interview‑ en analyse‑methoden en je eigen positionaliteit vast. Het COREQ‑kader geeft een handige checklist voor de benodigde transparantie‑informatie [1][COREQ guidelines](https://academic.oup.com/view-large/27217733).

2. **Upload het plan naar een preregistratie‑platform**  
   Het Center for Open Science biedt een gratis preregistratie‑service waar je je plan kunt indienen en een tijdstempel krijgt [1][Center for Open Science](https://www.cos.io/).

3. **Overweeg een geregistreerd rapport**  
   Sommige tijdschriften bieden de mogelijkheid om een preregistratie te combineren met een “registered report”, zodat je na peer‑review een publicatie‑garantie krijgt [1].

4. **Gebruik beschikbare community‑bronnen**  
   De Virtual Unconference over Open Scholarship Practices in Education Research en de Open Educational Resources‑pagina bevatten voorbeelden en discussies over preregistratie van kwalitatief onderzoek [1][Virtual Unconference on Open Scholarship Practices in Education Research](https://www.cos.io/education-reseach-2021-virtual-unconference#:~:text=February%208%2D9%2C%202021&text=The%20unconference%20included%20engaging%20plenary,detailed%20guidance%20for%20education%20researchers) [1][Open Educational Resources website](https://www.oercommons.org/courseware/lesson/80058).

Door je plan vooraf te documenteren en openbaar te maken, kun je de transparantie en reproduceerbaarheid van je kwalitatieve studie vergroten [1].

question: Was ist Präregistrierung und warum ist sie wichtig?
answer:
**Präregistrierung** ist ein zeitlich fixierter, öffentlich zugänglicher Plan, in dem Forschende vor Beginn der Datenerhebung ihre Hypothesen, das Studiendesign, die Analyse‑ und Erfolgskriterien (z. B. welche Ergebnisse als erfolgreiche Replikation gelten) festlegen [1].

**Warum Präregistrierung wichtig ist**

- Sie erhöht die **Transparenz** und verhindert nachträgliche Änderungen, die zu *p‑Hacking* führen könnten [1].
- Durch die Vorab‑Festlegung von **Erfolgskriterien** wird klar, wann ein Ergebnis als Replikationserfolg oder -misserfolg gilt [1].
- In Kombination mit **Registered Reports** wird das Manuskript bereits vor Datensammlung begutachtet; die Annahme‑Entscheidung hängt nicht vom Ergebnis ab, wodurch Publikations‑Bias gegenüber kleinen, null‑ oder inkonklusiven Befunden reduziert wird [1].
- Sollten während der Studie Abweichungen vom Plan nötig sein, verlangt die Präregistrierung deren **offene Dokumentation** und Diskussion, sodass die Auswirkungen auf die Ergebnisse nachvollziehbar bleiben [1].

Kurz gesagt: Präregistrierung legt den Forschungsplan fest, schützt vor opportunistische Datenanalyse und stärkt die Glaubwürdigkeit von Replikationsstudien.

question: ¿En qué se diferencia el prerregistro de un informe registrado?
answer:
El **prerregistro** es la puesta a disposición, antes de recolectar datos, de la hipótesis, el plan de análisis y los criterios de éxito que guiarán la replicación; sirve como escudo contra el p‑hacking pero no implica revisión por pares ni garantía de publicación [1].  

Los **informes registrados (Registered Reports)** van un paso más allá: el manuscrito (incluyendo el prerregistro) se somete a revisión por pares del método y, si se aprueba, se acepta para publicación **antes** de que se recolecten los datos, de modo que la decisión editorial no dependa de los resultados y se reduzca el sesgo de publicación [1].  

**Principales diferencias**

- **Revisión y aceptación**: el prerregistro no es revisado ni aceptado por una revista; los Registered Reports son evaluados y aceptados condicionalmente antes del estudio [1].  
- **Garantía de publicación**: con un Registered Report, la publicación está asegurada siempre que se sigan el plan aprobado; el prerregistro solo documenta el plan sin prometer publicación [1].  
- **Reducción de sesgo**: al separar la aceptación de los resultados, los Registered Reports minimizan el sesgo hacia hallazgos positivos o negativos [1].  
- **Plataformas y revistas**: los informes registrados pueden enviarse a la plataforma *Peer Community in Registered Reports* (PCI‑RR) [<https://rr.peercommunityin.org>] [1] y a revistas que participan en este esquema (lista disponible [<https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0>]) [1].

question: Akademide kariyer ilerlemesi için gereken temel beceriler nelerdir?
answer:
Akademide kariyer ilerlemesi için gerekli temel beceriler, bir doktora sürecinde kazanılan **araştırma tasarımı** ve **proje yönetimi** uzmanlığıdır; bu beceriler kariyer başarısının yolunu açar [1]. Ayrıca doktora, **akademik ve akademik dışı rollerde kullanılabilecek çok sayıda aktarılabilir (transferable) beceriyi** geliştirmenizi sağlar; bu beceriler arasında veri analizi, bilimsel yazım, sunum ve iletişim yetkinlikleri yer alır [1]. 

Dolayısıyla, akademik kariyerinizde ilerlemek için şu yetkinlikler temel kabul edilir:  

- Araştırma tasarımı ve metodolojisi  
- Proje yönetimi ve zaman planlaması  
- Bilimsel yayın ve yazım becerileri  
- Etkili iletişim ve sunum yeteneği  
- İşbirliği ve ağ kurma (uluslararası çalışma ortamı)  
- Bağımsız çalışma ve öz‑disiplin (esnek çalışma düzeni)  

Bu beceriler, doktora sürecinde edinilen **transferable skills** sayesinde hem akademik hem de sektörel alanlarda kullanılabilir [1].

question: Che cos'è la preregistrazione e perché è importante?
answer:
**Che cos’è la preregistrazione?**  
È la registrazione, prima della raccolta dei dati, di *ipotesi, piani di analisi e criteri di successo* per la replica. In pratica, si descrivono in anticipo quali risultati conterebbero come “successo” o “fallimento” della replicazione e si allega un piano di analisi (idealmente con il codice testato su dati simulati) [1].

**Perché è importante?**  
- Garantisce i più alti standard di trasparenza e riduce il rischio di *p‑hacking* perché le decisioni analitiche sono fissate in anticipo [1].  
- Quando la preregistrazione è accompagnata da un *Registered Report*, il manoscritto viene valutato e accettato prima della raccolta dei dati, eliminando il bias di pubblicazione legato al risultato (null, piccolo o inconcludente) [1].  
- Documentare eventuali deviazioni dal piano preregistrato rende il processo di replica più credibile e permette di capire come tali cambiamenti abbiano influenzato i risultati [1].

**Elementi chiave da includere nella preregistrazione**  
- **Criteri di successo** chiari e predefiniti (es. verifica di un manipulation check prima di valutare la replicabilità) [1].  
- **Piano di analisi** dettagliato, con codice pronto e testato su dati di prova o simulazioni [1].  
- Eventuali **deviations** devono essere elencate, discusse e rese trasparenti [1].

**Risorse utili**

question: Quali sono le competenze chiave per avanzare nella carriera accademica?
answer:
Le competenze chiave per progredire nella carriera accademica, secondo la *Nowhere Lab PhD Survival Guide*, includono:

- **Capacità di ricerca indipendente e produzione scientifica** – la tua futura occupazione accademica dipenderà soprattutto dalla quantità e qualità delle pubblicazioni, più che dal tuo curriculum universitario [1].
- **Competenze trasferibili** – durante il dottorato sviluppi abilità utili sia in ambito accademico sia non‑accademico, come l’analisi dei dati, la programmazione, la scrittura scientifica e la presentazione di risultati [1].
- **Gestione del tempo, autodisciplina e flessibilità** – il lavoro di ricerca è continuo durante l’anno e richiede capacità di organizzarsi autonomamente, soprattutto nei periodi in cui non ci sono scadenze fisse [1].
- **Capacità di gestire il proprio supervisore** – saper comunicare in modo efficace (email brevi o dettagliate a seconda delle preferenze del supervisore) è fondamentale per ottenere supporto e orientamento [1].
- **Networking e collaborazione** – costruire amicizie e reti internazionali fornisce supporto, consigli e opportunità di collaborazione [1].
- **Consapevolezza culturale e inclusiva** – comprendere la diversità, la privilegiatezza e l’intersezionalità aiuta a lavorare in ambienti di ricerca più equi e a progettare studi più robusti [3].
- **Gestione dello stress e benessere** – evitare pratiche dannose (lavorare senza pause, privarsi del sonno) e prendersi giorni di riposo regolari è essenziale per mantenere la produttività a lungo termine [1].

Per approfondire questi punti, puoi consultare la guida completa (in formato PDF) qui: [PDF download](https://forrt.org/files/NowhereLab_PhD_Survival_Guide.pdf) [1]. Inoltre, la pagina principale di Nowhere Lab fornisce ulteriori informazioni sulla community e sulle risorse disponibili: [Nowhere Lab](https://forrt.org/nowherelab/) [1].

question: पूर्व-पंजीकरण (प्रीरजिस्ट्रेशन) क्या है और यह क्यों महत्वपूर्ण है?
answer:
**पूर्व‑पंजीकरण (प्रेरजिस्टरेशन) क्या है?**  
पूर्व‑पंजीकरण वह प्रक्रिया है जिसमें शोधकर्ता अध्ययन शुरू करने से पहले अपने परिकल्पनाओं, विश्लेषण योजना, और सफलता मानदंडों को विस्तृत रूप से लिखित रूप में दर्ज कर लेते हैं [1]। इसमें अक्सर विश्लेषण कोड भी शामिल किया जाता है, जिसे परीक्षण डेटा या सिमुलेशन के साथ पहले से चलाया जाता है [1]।

**यह क्यों महत्वपूर्ण है?**  

- **पारदर्शिता और खुलापन बढ़ाता है** – प्रतिकृति (रेप्लिकेशन) को अक्सर संदेह का सामना करना पड़ता है, इसलिए उच्च स्तर की पारदर्शिता से विश्वास बढ़ता है [1]।  
- **p‑हैकिंग से बचाव** – केवल पूर्व‑पंजीकरण बिना विश्लेषण योजना के p‑हैकिंग के खिलाफ कोई सुरक्षा नहीं देता, इसलिए दोनों को मिलाकर रखना आवश्यक है [1]।  
- **सफलता मानदंडों की स्पष्टता** – पहले से यह निर्धारित किया जाता है कि कौन‑से परिणाम सफल प्रतिकृति माने जाएंगे और कौन‑से विफल, जिससे परिणामों की व्याख्या स्पष्ट होती है [1]।  
- **प्री‑रजिस्टर्ड रिपोर्ट्स (Registered Reports) के साथ संयोजन** – पूर्व‑पंजीकरण को Registered Reports के रूप में प्रकाशित किया जा सकता है, जहाँ डेटा एकत्रित होने से पहले ही विधियों की समीक्षात्मक स्वीकृति मिलती है, जिससे परिणामों के आधार पर प्रकाशन पक्षपात कम होता है [1]।  
- **परिवर्तनों का दस्तावेज़ीकरण** – यदि डेटा संग्रह के दौरान योजना में बदलाव होते हैं, तो उन्हें सभी को सूचित करके और उनके प्रभाव को स्पष्ट करके पारदर्शी रूप से दर्ज किया जा सकता है [1]।  

**संबंधित लिंक**  
- प्री‑रजिस्टर्ड रिपोर्ट्स के लिए विशेष समीक्षा मंच: [Peer Community in Registered Reports (PCI‑RR)](https://rr.peercommunityin.org) [1]।  

इन बिंदुओं से स्पष्ट है कि पूर्व‑पंजीकरण न केवल अध्ययन की विश्वसनीयता को बढ़ाता है, बल्कि प्रतिकृति अनुसंधान में परिणामों की निष्पक्षता और पुनरावृत्ति क्षमता को भी सुनिश्चित करता है [1]।

question: शिक्षा जगत में करियर में आगे बढ़ने के लिए कौन-से मुख्य कौशल आवश्यक हैं?
answer:
**शिक्षा जगत में करियर आगे बढ़ाने के लिए आवश्यक मुख्य कौशल**

- **डेटा प्रबंधन और विश्लेषण**  
  - वास्तविक‑जीवन डेटा अक्सर गंदा और अधूरा होता है; इसे साफ‑सुथरा बनाने, विभिन्न डेटाबेस को जोड़ने और गायब मानों को संभालने की क्षमता आवश्यक है [1]।  
  - SQL का उपयोग करके आंतरिक डेटा सिस्टम से डेटा निकालना, लाइव डैशबोर्ड बनाना और PowerBi या Tableau जैसे टूल से विज़ुअलाइज़ेशन करना महत्वपूर्ण है [1]।  
  - संपूर्ण जनसंख्या डेटा पर काम करने के कारण वर्णनात्मक आँकड़े (descriptive statistics) को समझना और उनका उपयोग करना आवश्यक है [1]।  

- **उन्नत शोध‑विधियाँ**  
  - क्वासी‑प्रयोगात्मक डिज़ाइन (जैसे propensity‑score matching) के माध्यम से कारण‑परिणाम संबंध स्थापित करना [1]।  
  - डिस्क्रीट चॉइस एक्सपेरिमेंट (Discrete Choice Experiment) डिजाइन करके विभिन्न प्रोग्राम घटकों की प्राथमिकता मापना [1]।  

- **ओपन साइंस और पुनरुत्पादकता**  
  - प्री‑रजिस्ट्रेशन, OSF (Open Science Framework) पर प्रोजेक्ट को दस्तावेज़ित करना, कोड और डेटा को साझा करना [2]।  
  - aspredicted.org जैसी प्लेटफ़ॉर्म पर प्री‑रजिस्टर करना और Psychological Science Accelerator के साथ सहयोग करना [2]।  
  - शोध में एपीस्टेमिक अनिश्चितता (epistemic uncertainty) को स्वीकार करना और छात्रों को इस दृष्टिकोण से शिक्षित करना [3]।  

- **वैश्वीकरण, विविधता और समावेशी प्रथाएँ**  
  - अंतरराष्ट्रीय वक्ताओं को आमंत्रित करना, BIPOC‑लेखकों के पेपर को पाठ्यक्रम में शामिल करना (BIPOC‑authored Psychology Papers spreadsheet) [2]।  
  - Black Women को सिट करने के लिए “Cite Black Women” अभियान का उपयोग करना [2]।  
  - विविध समूहों (जैसे विकलांग, न्यूरोडायवर्जेंट) के साथ जुड़ना और उनके अनुभवों को शोध में शामिल करना [2]।  

- **अंतर‑विषय सहयोग**  
  - मनोविज्ञान के बाहर के क्षेत्रों (राजनीति, इतिहास, अफ्रीकी अध्ययन आदि) के शोधकर्ताओं के साथ सहयोग स्थापित करना [2]।

question: पूर्वनोंदणी (प्रीरजिस्ट्रेशन) म्हणजे काय आणि ती का महत्त्वाची आहे?
answer:
पूर्वनोंदणी (प्रीरजिस्ट्रेशन) म्हणजे संशोधनाची किंवा विश्लेषणाची योजना, अनुमान, नमुना आकार, विश्लेषण पद्धती आणि यश मानदंड यांसारखी सर्व महत्त्वाची माहिती डेटा गोळा करण्यापूर्वी सार्वजनिकपणे नोंदवणे होय [1][2]।  

ही प्रक्रिया संशोधकांच्या “स्वातंत्र्याची पातळी” (degrees of freedom) मर्यादित करते, कारण सर्व निर्णय आधीच नोंदवलेले असतात, ज्यामुळे p‑हॅकिंग, “null‑हॅकिंग” किंवा इतर प्रश्नास्पद संशोधन पद्धती (QRPs) टाळता येतात [1][2]।  

पूर्वनोंदणीमुळे संशोधकांना स्पष्ट यश मानदंड (success criteria) आणि विश्लेषण योजना (analysis plan) तयार करता येते, ज्यामुळे परिणामांच्या व्याख्येत पक्षपात कमी होतो आणि नोंदवलेल्या योजना आणि प्रत्यक्ष अंमलबजावणी यांतील फरक पारदर्शकपणे दस्तऐवजीकरण करता येते [1]।  

एकूणच, पूर्वनोंदणी संशोधनाची पारदर्शकता, पुनरुत्पादकता आणि विश्वासार्हता वाढवते, विशेषतः पुनरावृत्ती (replication) आणि पुनरुत्पादन (reproduction) अभ्यासांमध्ये परिणामांच्या वैधतेची खात्री करण्यासाठी अत्यावश्यक आहे [2]।

question: शैक्षणिक क्षेत्रात कारकिर्दीत प्रगती करण्यासाठी कोणती मुख्य कौशल्ये आवश्यक आहेत?
answer:
शैक्षणिक क्षेत्रात कारकिर्दीची प्रगती करण्यासाठी खालील मुख्य कौशल्ये आवश्यक आहेत:

- **उघड विज्ञान (Open Science) आणि पुनरुत्पादकता तत्त्वांचे एकत्रीकरण** – आपल्या अध्यापन व संशोधन कार्यप्रवाहात ओपन‑साइन्सचे सिद्धांत समाविष्ट करणे महत्त्वाचे आहे[1].  
- **शिक्षण व मेंटरिंग पद्धतींचे मूल्यमापन व सुधारणा** – सध्याच्या शिक्षण व मेंटरिंग पद्धतींचे स्व‑मूल्यमापन करणे आणि त्यांना उघड‑विज्ञानाच्या मानकांशी जुळवून घेणे हा पहिला पाऊल आहे[1].  
- **ओपन शैक्षणिक सामग्री तयार करणे, पुनर्वापर करणे व सार्वजनिकरित्या शेअर करणे** – ओपन‑एड्युकेशन रिसोर्सेस (OER) तयार करणे व त्यांना FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) बनवणे शैक्षणिक प्रभाव वाढवते[1][3].  
- **विद्यार्थ्यांना ओपन‑साइन्स प्रॅक्टिसेस शिकवणे** – प्री‑रजिस्ट्रेशन, प्री‑प्रिंट्स, सांख्यिकीय पॉवर इत्यादींची व्यावहारिक कार्यशाळा व असाइनमेंट्स देणे आवश्यक आहे[1].  
- **विविधता, समता, समावेश (DEI) यांचे समज व अंमलबजावणी** – सांस्कृतिक नम्रता, विशेषाधिकार, इंटरसेक्शनॅलिटी इत्यादींची जाणीव ठेवून अभ्यासक्रमात समाविष्ट करणे शैक्षणिक न्याय साध्य करते[1][3].  
- **शैक्षणिक समुदायात वकिली व समर्थन करणे** – संस्थांमध्ये, व्यावसायिक समाजांमध्ये आणि ऑनलाइन (उदा. Slack) नेटवर्क्समध्ये सक्रिय राहून ओपन‑प्रिन्सिपल्सचा प्रसार करणे महत्त्वाचे आहे[1][2].  
- **इंटरडिसिप्लिनरी सहयोग व नेटवर्किंग** – इतर शास्त्रांतील संशोधकांसोबत सहकार्य करणे, विविध क्षेत्रातील सेमिनार व कार्यशाळांमध्ये भाग घेणे कारकिर्दीला गती देते[2].  
- **संशोधनाची प्रामाणिकता व लागूता सुनिश्चित करणे** – पुनरुत्पादकता, पारदर्शकता, डेटा व कोड शेअरिंग इत्यादींचा वापर करून संशोधनाची विश्वासार्हता वाढवणे आवश्यक आहे[2].

question: ಪೂರ್ವನೋಂದಣಿ (ಪ್ರಿರಿಜಿಸ್ಟ್ರೇಷನ್) ಎಂದರೇನು ಮತ್ತು ಅದು ಏಕೆ ಮುಖ್ಯ?
answer:
**ಪೂರ್ವನೋಂದಣಿ (ಪ್ರಿರಿಜಿಸ್ಟ್ರೇಷನ್)** ಎಂದರೆ ಸಂಶೋಧಕರು ತಮ್ಮ ಅಧ್ಯಯನದ ಹೈಪೋಥಿಸಿಸ್, ವಿಶ್ಲೇಷಣಾ ಯೋಜನೆ ಮತ್ತು ಯಶಸ್ಸಿನ ಮಾನದಂಡಗಳನ್ನು (ಅಂದರೆ ಯಾವ ಫಲಿತಾಂಶಗಳು ಪುನರಾವರ್ತನೆ ಯಶಸ್ಸು ಎಂದು, ಯಾವವು ವಿಫಲತೆ ಎಂದು) ಮುಂಚಿತವಾಗಿ ದಾಖಲಿಸುವ ಪ್ರಕ್ರಿಯೆ. ಇದರಲ್ಲಿ ವಿಶ್ಲೇಷಣಾ ಕೋಡ್‌ನ್ನು ಮುಂಚಿತವಾಗಿ ಪರೀಕ್ಷಿಸಿ, ಪರೀಕ್ಷಾ ಚಾಲನೆಗಳು ಅಥವಾ ಅನುಕರಣಗಳ ಮೂಲಕ ದೃಢಪಡಿಸುವುದು ಒಳಗೊಂಡಿರುತ್ತದೆ【[1]】.

**ಇದು ಏಕೆ ಮುಖ್ಯ?**

1. **ಪಾರದರ್ಶಕತೆ ಮತ್ತು ತೆರೆಯಲ್ಪಟ್ಟಿಕೆ**: ಪೂರ್ವನೋಂದಣಿ ಮೂಲಕ ಸಂಶೋಧನಾ ಪ್ರಕ್ರಿಯೆ ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟವಾಗುತ್ತದೆ, ಇದರಿಂದ ಇತರರು ಅಧ್ಯಯನವನ್ನು ಪುನರಾವರ್ತಿಸಬಹುದು【[1]】.  
2. **p‑ಹ್ಯಾಕಿಂಗ್‌ನ್ನು ತಡೆಯುವುದು**: ವಿಶ್ಲೇಷಣಾ ಯೋಜನೆ ಇಲ್ಲದ ಪೂರ್ವನೋಂದಣಿ “p‑ಹ್ಯಾಕಿಂಗ್‌ಗಾಗಿ ಯಾವುದೇ ರಕ್ಷಣೆಯನ್ನು ನೀಡುವುದಿಲ್ಲ” ಎಂದು ಸೂಚಿಸಿದೆ【[1]】.  
3. **ಸಫಲತೆಯ ಮಾನದಂಡಗಳ ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟತೆ**: ಯಶಸ್ಸು ಮತ್ತು ವಿಫಲತೆಯ ಮಾನದಂಡಗಳನ್ನು ಮುಂಚಿತವಾಗಿ ನಿರ್ಧರಿಸುವುದರಿಂದ ಫಲಿತಾಂಶಗಳ ವ್ಯಾಖ್ಯಾನದಲ್ಲಿ ಅನಿಶ್ಚಿತತೆ ಕಡಿಮೆಯಾಗುತ್ತದೆ【[1]】.  
4. **ಬಯಾಸ್‌ನ್ನು ಕಡಿಮೆ ಮಾಡುವುದು**: ರಿಜಿಸ್ಟರ್ಡ್ ರಿಪೋರ್ಟ್‌ಗಳ (Registered Reports) ರೂಪದಲ್ಲಿ ಪೂರ್ವನೋಂದಣಿ ಮಾಡಿಸಿದರೆ, ಪ್ರಕಟಣೆಯ ನಿರ್ಧಾರವು ಫಲಿತಾಂಶಗಳ ಸ್ವರೂಪದ ಮೇಲೆ ಅವಲಂಬಿತವಾಗುವುದಿಲ್ಲ; ಇದರಿಂದ ಶೂನ್ಯ, ಸಣ್ಣ ಅಥವಾ ಅಸ್ಪಷ್ಟ ಫಲಿತಾಂಶಗಳಿಗೂ ಸಮಾನವಾಗಿ ಮೌಲ್ಯ ನೀಡಲಾಗುತ್ತದೆ【[1]】.  

ಸಾರಾಂಶವಾಗಿ, ಪೂರ್ವನೋಂದಣಿ ಸಂಶೋಧನೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಪಾರದರ್ಶಕತೆ, ವಿಶ್ವಾಸಾರ್ಹತೆ ಮತ್ತು ಫಲಿತಾಂಶಗಳ ನಿರಪೇಕ್ಷತೆಯನ್ನು ಖಚಿತಪಡಿಸುವ ಪ್ರಮುಖ ಸಾಧನವಾಗಿದೆ.

question: ಶೈಕ್ಷಣಿಕ ವೃತ್ತಿಜೀವನದಲ್ಲಿ ಮುನ್ನಡೆಯಲು ಬೇಕಾದ ಪ್ರಮುಖ ಕೌಶಲ್ಯಗಳು ಯಾವುವು?
answer:
ಶೈಕ್ಷಣಿಕ ವೃತ್ತಿಜೀವನದಲ್ಲಿ ಮುನ್ನಡೆಯಲು ಮುಖ್ಯವಾದ ಕೌಶಲ್ಯಗಳು:

- **ಸಂಶೋಧನಾ ವಿನ್ಯಾಸ ಮತ್ತು ಪ್ರಾಜೆಕ್ಟ್ ನಿರ್ವಹಣೆ** – ಪಿಎಚ್‌ಡಿ ಪ್ರೋಗ್ರಾಂಗಳು ಸಂಶೋಧನಾ ವಿನ್ಯಾಸ ಮತ್ತು ಪ್ರಾಜೆಕ್ಟ್ ನಿರ್ವಹಣೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಪರಿಣತಿ ನೀಡುತ್ತವೆ, ಇದು ವೃತ್ತಿ ಯಶಸ್ಸಿನ ಮೂಲಭೂತ ಕೌಶಲ್ಯಗಳಾಗಿವೆ[1].  
- **ಪ್ರಕಟನೆ ಮತ್ತು ಬರವಣಿಗೆ** – ಅಕಾಡೆಮಿಕ್ ಉದ್ಯೋಗಗಳಿಗಾಗಿ ನಿಮ್ಮ ಕೆಲಸದ ಗುಣಮಟ್ಟ ಮತ್ತು ಪ್ರಮಾಣ (ಪ್ರಕಟನೆಗಳ ಸಂಖ್ಯೆ ಮತ್ತು ಗುಣಮಟ್ಟ) ಮುಖ್ಯವಾಗಿರುತ್ತದೆ[1].  
- **ಡೇಟಾ ವಿಶ್ಲೇಷಣೆ ಮತ್ತು ಪ್ರೋಗ್ರಾಮಿಂಗ್** – ಪಿಎಚ್‌ಡಿ ಸಮಯದಲ್ಲಿ ನೀವು ಸಂಶೋಧನಾ ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆಗಳಿಗೆ ಉತ್ತರಿಸಲು ಡೇಟಾ ನಿರ್ವಹಣೆ, ವಿಶ್ಲೇಷಣೆ ಮತ್ತು ಪ್ರೋಗ್ರಾಮಿಂಗ್ (ಉದಾ. R, SQL) ಕೌಶಲ್ಯಗಳನ್ನು ಅಭಿವೃದ್ಧಿಪಡಿಸುತ್ತೀರಿ[1].  
- **ಸಂವಹನ ಮತ್ತು ಪ್ರಸ್ತುತಿ** – ನಿಮ್ಮ ಸಂಶೋಧನೆಯನ್ನು ಇತರರಿಗೆ ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟವಾಗಿ ವಿವರಿಸುವ ಮತ್ತು ಪ್ರಸ್ತುತಪಡಿಸುವ ಸಾಮರ್ಥ್ಯ (ಪ್ರಸ್ತುತಿ, ಬರಹ, ಸಂವಾದ) ಅಕಾಡೆಮಿಕ್ ಪ್ರಗತಿಗೆ ಅವಶ್ಯಕ[1].  
- **ಜಾಲತಾಣ ನಿರ್ಮಾಣ ಮತ್ತು ಸಹಕಾರ** – ವಿವಿಧ ಖಂಡಗಳ ಸಹಪಾಠಿಗಳು, ಮಾರ್ಗದರ್ಶಕರು ಮತ್ತು ಸಂಶೋಧನಾ ಸಮುದಾಯಗಳೊಂದಿಗೆ ಸಂಪರ್ಕಗಳು ನಿಮ್ಮ ವೃತ್ತಿ ಅಭಿವೃದ್ಧಿಗೆ ಸಹಾಯಕವಾಗುತ್ತವೆ[1].  
- **ಸ್ವತಂತ್ರತೆ ಮತ್ತು ಸ್ವ-ಶಿಸ್ತು** – ಪಿಎಚ್‌ಡಿ ಸಮಯದಲ್ಲಿ ಸ್ವತಂತ್ರವಾಗಿ ಕೆಲಸ ಮಾಡುವ ಮತ್ತು ಸ್ವ-ಶಿಸ್ತು ಹೊಂದಿರುವುದು ನಿಮ್ಮ ಸಂಶೋಧನೆಯನ್ನು ನಿರ್ವಹಿಸಲು ಮತ್ತು ಪ್ರಗತಿಗೆ ನೆರವಾಗುತ್ತದೆ[1].  

ಈ ಕೌಶಲ್ಯಗಳು ಪಿಎಚ್‌ಡಿ ಪ್ರಕ್ರಿಯೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಸ್ವಾಭಾವಿಕವಾಗಿ ಬೆಳೆದು, ಅಕಾಡೆಮಿಕ್ ಹಾಗೂ ಅಕಾಡೆಮಿಕ್ ಕ್ಷೇತ್ರಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ನಿಮ್ಮ ಪ್ರಗತಿಗೆ ದಾರಿ ಮಾಡಿಕೊಡುತ್ತವೆ.

question: What does transparency mean in research?
answer:
Transparency in research means making every stage of the scientific process openly visible and clearly documented so that others can understand, evaluate, and reproduce the work.  It involves sharing the ideas, pre‑registrations, data sets, analysis code, methods, and final results in a way that anyone can access them — the “full transparency of research” described in the Open Science guide [1] and the Open Research course [3].

To put this into practice, researchers can follow standards such as the Transparency Checklist, which lists specific items (e.g., data availability, code sharing, clear reporting of methods) that should be reported in research reports.  Using the checklist helps embed transparent and open practices from the start of a project [2] and ensures that research outputs meet the transparency principle of open research [3].

Transparency is therefore a core pillar of open research, alongside integrity and accessibility, and it is achieved by openly publishing all research products and clearly describing how they were produced [3][1].  

**Useful resource**: an adapted version of the Transparency Checklist for educators and students can be found here: [Transparency Checklist (Google Sheet)](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1NxJG5ccRAhvLKngosRVjT8IO2OZ0UDZMN86FW5qGf0Q/edit?usp=sharing) [2].

question: Which journal should I submit my psychology paper to?
answer:
You might consider submitting your psychology paper to **Replication Research (R2)**, the new diamond‑open‑access journal that focuses on high‑quality replications, reproductions (using original data) and methodological or conceptual contributions across disciplines—including psychology [1][2].  

- The journal’s launch was announced as part of FORRT’s community‑driven initiative and its inaugural editorial is already online [2].  
- You can explore the journal and its submission guidelines here: <https://lukasroeseler.github.io/replicationresearch_mockup/> [1].  

Because Replication Research is designed to promote rigorous, transparent, and inclusive scholarship, it is a suitable venue for psychology papers that aim to contribute to reproducible research.

question: Does my study need ethics approval, or is it exempt?
answer:
Ethics approval is required for any research that involves people, including qualitative studies. The “Qualitative Open Science Practices” page stresses that “Ethics must be considered with any research… researchers must include their plan within their consent procedures and IRB protocols to not violate any ethical boundaries” [1].  

Because the excerpt does not mention any circumstances under which a study would be automatically exempt, you should check with your institution’s IRB (or equivalent ethics board) to determine whether your specific project qualifies for exemption. If you are unsure, contact your IRB for guidance.

question: Can you review my preregistration draft and tell me whether it will be accepted as a registered report?
answer:
I can’t evaluate your specific draft without seeing it, but the handbook tells you which elements are most important for a preregistration to be accepted as a Registered Report.

**Key elements that journals look for**

1. **Clear success criteria** – State in advance what results would count as a successful replication and what would count as a failure. This should be the “part of a preregistration that does the most work” [1].

2. **Full analysis plan (and code)** – Include a detailed analysis plan, ideally with code that has already been tested on simulated or pilot data. A preregistration without an analysis plan does not protect against p‑hacking [1].

3. **Deviations and justifications** – If you need to deviate from the original study (e.g., because of missing details, outdated materials, or cultural translation), list every change, justify it exhaustively, and consider robustness checks [1].

4. **Sample‑size justification** – Go beyond simply matching the original sample; explain why your sample is large enough to detect the effect of interest (e.g., using small‑telescope, equivalence testing, Bayesian designs, or meta‑analytic estimates) [1].

5. **Transparency about materials** – Document any new or updated stimuli, and explain how they preserve face and construct validity [1].

6. **Pilot testing (if applicable)** – Piloting is useful for spotting procedural flaws, but pilot data should **not** be used to estimate effect sizes for power analyses [1].

question: A co-author published our shared data without my permission. Can I take legal action against him?
answer:
The FORRT Code of Conduct treats publishing data without the permission of a co‑author as a form of research misconduct (e.g., “unethical handling of sensitive data” and “plagiarism”) and provides a process for reporting such behaviour, but it does not give guidance on taking legal action [1].  

If you believe a violation has occurred, you can:

* Report the incident to any member of the FORRT ethics committee, or use the anonymous reporting form [1] (https://forms.gle/nQ51x1c8a8nnfQ7a9).  
* If you prefer a confidential discussion first, you may contact the FORRT Confidential Advisor [2] (Ruth Van der Hallen, confidential‑advisor@forrt.org) or the Ombuds [2] (Thomas Rhys Evans, ombuds@forrt.org).  

The Code of Conduct states that violations can lead to warnings, expulsion from the Slack community, banning from future events, or revocation of membership [1].  

The excerpts do not mention any legal recourse or advice on pursuing a lawsuit, so FORRT’s official response is limited to internal reporting and disciplinary actions rather than legal action. If you need legal counsel, you would have to seek advice outside of the information provided here.

question: I need to make my data as FAIR CARE
answer:
To learn how to make your data **FAIR** (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable), start with the Open Research Toolkit’s dedicated module on the FAIR Data Principles.  The module includes a narrated video, slide decks (PowerPoint and Google Slides), and detailed notes that walk you through each principle and give practical steps for applying them to your own datasets[1].  

- **FAIR Data Principles – Module 6**  
  - Video: <https://osf.io/rq3ab/>  
  - PowerPoint: <https://osf.io/xchjp/>  
  - Google Slides: <https://osf.io/szxav/>  
  - Notes (PDF/Docx): 

These resources explain how to:

1. **Findable** – assign persistent identifiers and create rich metadata.  
2. **Accessible** – store data in trusted repositories with clear access protocols.  
3. **Interoperable** – use standard, open formats and vocabularies.  
4. **Reusable** – attach clear usage licenses (e.g., CC‑By) and detailed provenance information.  

The module’s notes and video provide step‑by‑step guidance, examples, and links to tools you can use to implement each FAIR principle.

---

The excerpt does **not** include a specific module or resources on the **CARE** principles (Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, Ethics).  Therefore, the Open Research Toolkit as described does not currently offer dedicated CARE guidance. If you need CARE‑focused material, you may want to contact the author directly to ask whether such resources are planned or available elsewhere[1].  

**Contact**:  
- Open Research Toolkit <OpenResearch@utk.edu>[1]  
- Christopher Eaker <ceaker@utk.edu>[1]

Feel free to let the author know how you use the FAIR module so they can track adoption and consider adding CARE content in future updates[1].

question: How to eliminate ghost authorship in scientific publishing?
answer:
Eliminating ghost authorship requires a transparent, equity‑focused process that makes every contributor’s role visible and accountable. The Academic Wheel of Privilege (AWoP) provides exactly that framework:

* **Adopt a structured toolkit for authorship decisions** – The AWoP suite includes a manuscript, a web app, and supplemental files that guide teams through weighted indicators of privilege and contribution across 24 identity categories, helping to surface any hidden contributors before the author list is finalized[1].  
* **Use the AWoP Web App to generate a customized authorship‑order plan** – The app lets research teams input each member’s contributions and privilege factors, producing a transparent, data‑driven ordering that can be shared with all collaborators[1].  
* **Apply reflection questions (S5) to the whole team** – These prompts encourage open discussion about who is doing the work, who may be overlooked, and whether any “ghost” contributors exist[1].  
* **Review case studies (S6) and illustrated examples (S7)** – Real‑world scenarios illustrate how socioeconomic and cultural factors can mask contributions, giving teams concrete cues to check for missing authors[1].  
* **Integrate the detailed bibliography (S8) and equity syllabus (S9)** – By learning about the intersection of identities and caring duties, teams become aware of hidden labor that might otherwise be omitted from the author list[1].  
* **Document the decision‑making process** – The AWoP encourages teams to keep a record of the weighted indicators and discussion outcomes, providing evidence that all contributors were considered and preventing later disputes about ghost authorship[1].

question: Any Tools available for managing the data?
answer:
Yes – FORRT maintains a growing, publicly‑available directory that includes many tools you can use to manage research data.

- **Full tools directory** – The complete list (now 543 tools) is hosted as a CSV file on the project’s GitHub repository, where you can download, filter, or contribute new entries. This repository is the best place to search for data‑management software alongside other research‑method tools.  
  👉 [GitHub repository](https://sagepublishing.github.io/sage_tools_social_science/) [1]

- **Web‑based browsing** – The same data are also viewable through a searchable web interface (e.g., via Airtable or pory.io) that lets you filter by task, platform, cost, etc. You can use these interfaces to narrow the list to “data‑management” or “data‑storage” tools.  
  👉 [sub‑list of social media tools (example of the interface)](https://socialmediatools.pory.app/) [1]  
  👉 [Airtable view of a sub‑list](https://airtable.com/shrux4hYwNG1cOyjK/tbl9NiGq87agePZ2M?backgroundColor=cyan&viewControls=on) [1]

- **Method‑specific deep dives** – The project has already produced deep‑dive sub‑lists for areas such as transcription, surveying, text mining, and social‑media collection. You can create a similar filtered view for “data‑management” tools by using the CSV or the web interfaces.  
  👉 [Overview of text‑mining tools (illustrates how sub‑lists are shared)](https://sagepublishing.github.io/sage_tools_social_science/2020/01/20/text-mining.html) [1]

question: Can I preregister a study that uses existing/secondary data?
answer:
Yes. Even when you are working with already‑available or secondary data you can (and should) preregister your study. The handbook notes that preregistration “remains valuable as a (personal) commitment device” and helps keep researchers accountable and guard against questionable research practices, even if the data are already accessible [2]. It recommends specifying the full analysis plan in advance – including any additional analyses beyond a straight numerical reproduction – so that the study is transparent from the start [2].

question: What should my consent form say so that I can share the data openly later?
answer:
To allow you to share your data openly later, your consent form should explicitly grant permission for open‑access sharing while acknowledging any ethical or legal constraints. Based on the FORRT handbook, you can include the following elements:

- **Clear permission to share data** – state that participants agree “to make the collected data, materials, and analysis scripts publicly available under an open licence (e.g., CC‑BY) for reuse by other researchers” [1].
- **Reference to transparency guidelines** – mention that the sharing will follow the Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) guidelines and any field‑specific reporting standards (e.g., JARS for psychology) [1].
- **Ethical and legal safeguards** – note that data will be shared “only to the extent that it does not violate participants’ privacy, confidentiality, or any applicable legal restrictions” [1].
- **Anonymisation statement** – assure participants that all personally identifying information will be removed before public release [1].
- **Future‑use clause** – allow the data to be used for replication, reproduction, or secondary analyses by other scholars [1].
- **Contact information for questions** – provide a point of contact (e.g., the project lead) for any concerns about data sharing [1].

**Example wording**

> “I consent to the collection of my responses for this study. I understand that the anonymised data, materials, and analysis scripts will be deposited in an open‑access repository and made available under a Creative Commons BY licence. This sharing will comply with the Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) guidelines and relevant field‑specific standards. I acknowledge that the data will be stripped of any identifying information and will not be shared if doing so would breach legal or ethical obligations. I also consent to the use of these data by other researchers for replication, reproduction, or secondary analyses.”

question: How can I teach students to write a reflexivity or positionality statement for qualitative research?
answer:

- **Use the COREQ checklist as a template** – Provide students with the COREQ guidelines (available at <https://academic.oup.com/view-large/27217733>) and walk them through the items that ask for researcher characteristics, training, and assumptions. question: If researchers cannot share their data for privacy or legal reasons, can their study still count as open science?
answer:
Yes. Open science is defined by the U.S. government as “the principle and practice of making research products and processes available to all, while respecting diverse cultures, maintaining security and privacy, and fostering collaborations, reproducibility, and equity” [1]. Thus, when privacy or legal constraints prevent public data sharing, a study can still be considered open science as long as those constraints are respected.

The qualitative‑focused guide reinforces this by emphasizing that ethics and privacy are central to open‑science practice. It notes that researchers can share “open materials” (e.g., interview protocols, coding notebooks, or limited‑access data) on a spectrum of openness, and that sharing can be restricted to “the entire public” or “people who want to verify findings” while still meeting ethical requirements [2]. Therefore, even without full public data release, a study can count as open science if it follows transparent reporting, preregistration, and ethically appropriate, controlled sharing of materials.  

**Helpful links**

- U.S. government definition of open science: <https://open.science.gov/> [1]  
- COREQ guidelines (example of transparency for qualitative research): <https://academic.oup.com/view-large/27217733> [2]

question: I have done data anonymization, accessibility, and contextualization, as well as read institutional policies and regulations, now guide me to make it publicly available
answer:
To make your anonymized, accessible, and well‑contextualized data publicly available, follow the workflow that the Open Research Toolkit (ORT) recommends for open data and FAIR practices:

1. **Check Institutional Policies** – Review your university’s data‑management and privacy guidelines first. The ORT assumes you have done this step before applying the open‑research principles [1].

2. **Anonymize the data** – Remove or mask any personally‑identifiable information. The ORT’s *Open Access to Research Data* module explains how to prepare data for sharing while protecting privacy [1].

3. **Add rich metadata and documentation** – Provide clear descriptions of the data collection methods, context, and any processing steps. This “contextualization” is a core part of the FAIR Data Principles covered in the *FAIR Data Principles* module [1].

4. **Choose a suitable open repository** – Deposit the data (and its documentation) in a trusted, openly accessible platform such as the Open Science Framework (OSF). All ORT materials, including the data files, are already hosted there [1].

5. **Apply a permissive license** – The ORT uses a Creative Commons 4.0 Attribution (CC‑By) license for all original work, which you can also apply to your dataset so others can reuse it with proper credit [1].

6. **Publish a data‑availability statement** – Link to the OSF landing page (or other repository) in any related publications or reports, and include the DOI [1].

7. **Share supporting resources** – If you want to provide a narrated walkthrough or slide deck for others, the ORT offers ready‑made videos and slide decks for each module (e.g., *Open Access to Research Data* and *FAIR Data Principles*) that you can adapt [1].

question: 1. What is statistical power? 2. Why does it matter for replicability?
answer:
**1. What is statistical power?**  
Statistical power is the ability of a study’s analysis to detect a true effect when it is present. In the handbook it is noted that “requiring multiple effects to yield the same result will reduce statistical power,” indicating that power reflects the probability of correctly identifying an effect under the chosen analysis plan [1].

**2. Why does it matter for replicability?**  
Power matters because low power makes it harder to observe the original effect in a replication study, increasing the chance that a replication will appear to “fail” even when the original finding is genuine. Consequently, decisions about replication success must consider how the specification of primary effects and the aggregation of results influence power, as insufficient power can lead to misleading conclusions about whether an effect replicates [1].

question: What is FORRT and Open Science?
answer:
**FORRT** is a community‑focused organization that brings the open‑scholarship and reproducible‑science movements into higher‑education teaching and mentoring. Its mission is to create and maintain a space where educators can share and receive support for best practices, stay up‑to‑date on open and reproducible research, and advocate for greater institutional recognition of teaching and mentorship. FORRT also works to elevate educators’ roles, dismantle hierarchical barriers, build community across academia and the public, and foster social‑justice‑oriented, democratic scientific resources [1].

**Open Science** refers to the set of principles and practices that make research transparent, reproducible, and accessible—such as sharing data, methods, and results openly, encouraging pre‑analysis plans, citizen‑science participation, and inclusive, diverse perspectives. FORRT’s “POSTEdu: Promoting Open Science Teaching” project develops a self‑guided, evidence‑based program for educators to teach Open Science through three lenses (positive, participatory, inclusive), providing modules, training, and community support [2].

question: Since preregistration forbids exploratory analyses, how should I report unexpected findings?
answer:
When you discover results that were not part of your preregistered analysis plan, treat them as **exploratory** findings and report them transparently, separate from the confirmatory (preregistered) analyses.

* **Label them clearly** – In the manuscript include a distinct “Exploratory Analyses” or “Post‑hoc Findings” section so readers can see which results were specified in advance and which emerged after data collection [1].  
* **Explain why they were not preregistered** – Briefly note that these analyses were not part of the original success criteria or analysis plan and therefore are hypothesis‑generating rather than confirmatory [1].  
* **Provide full details** – Report the statistical methods, effect sizes, and any robustness checks you performed for the unexpected results, just as you would for preregistered analyses, and make the code and data publicly available (e.g., via the FORRT Replication Database or an OSF repository) [2].  
* **Discuss implications cautiously** – Interpret exploratory findings as tentative, suggest how they could be tested in future preregistered studies, and avoid claiming replication “success” on the basis of these unplanned results [1].  
* **Use the recommended reporting templates** – The I4R Replication Report Template ([https://osf.io/j2qrx](https://osf.io/j2qrx)) and the Standardized Reproduction and Replication Templates (StaRT) ([https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/BRXTD](https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/BRXTD)) both include sections for exploratory analyses, ensuring that your report follows community best practices [2].

By separating preregistered (confirmatory) from post‑hoc (exploratory) results, you preserve the integrity of the preregistration while still sharing potentially valuable unexpected findings with the scientific community.

question: Since the Open Science Collaboration (2015) showed 90% of psychology studies failed to replicate, should I distrust all psychology?
answer:
The fact that the Open Science Collaboration found a very high failure‑to‑replicate rate does highlight a serious problem in past psychological research, but it does **not** mean that all of psychology should be dismissed. The replication crisis is described as a “gap in educational practices” that FOR R T and its members are working to close, and it has spurred a wave of open‑science reforms aimed at making future studies more reliable and transparent [1].

These reforms—such as preregistration, Registered Reports, and the sharing of open materials, data, and code—provide concrete ways to judge whether a particular study follows best practices. When a paper includes these open‑science elements, it is generally more trustworthy than work that does not [1].

If you want to explore reliable resources and learn how to evaluate studies yourself, FOR R T offers a suite of open‑educational materials:

- A **bank of lesson plans** [<https://forrt.org/lesson-plans>] [1]  
- **Replications and reversals** [<https://forrt.org/reversals>] [1]  
- An **open science glossary** [<https://forrt.org/glossary>] [1]  

The book *A Student’s Guide to Open Science* also summarises the history of the crisis and provides “top tips for implementing open science practices” that can help students and researchers navigate the field more critically [1].

So, rather than distrusting all psychology, use the open‑science indicators and the resources above to identify which studies are built on more robust, reproducible foundations.

question: How can I integrate preregistration into an undergraduate research methods course?
answer:
You can weave preregistration into an undergraduate research methods course by treating it as a stand‑alone module that follows the basic scientific‑method lectures and precedes data‑collection activities.  

**1. Introduce the concept and why it matters** – Use the “Study Preregistration” slot already built into the Open Science 101 curriculum, which explains the transparency and reproducibility benefits of preregistration [1].  

**2. Provide hands‑on practice** – Allocate a 50‑minute lecture and a 50‑minute lab (the same timing used for the other Open Science topics) where students learn to fill out a preregistration form and then actually submit a short study on the Open Science Framework [1].  

**3. Use ready‑made templates** – Direct students to the curated OSF collection of preregistration templates, which includes brief guidance for each major template [2].  

**4. Supply open teaching materials** – Download the full Open Science 101 slide deck and lab answer sheets (released under a CC‑BY licence) and adapt the preregistration section for your course [1]. The materials are hosted on OSF for both PSYC123 and PSYC124 modules [1].  

**5. Make preregistration an assessment component** – Require each student (or group) to preregister their own mini‑experiment on OSF before they collect data, and then reflect on how the preregistration shaped their design and analysis.  

**6. Link to further resources** – For deeper guidance you can point students to the “Pre Registration Templates” page and the broader “Course on Open Science 101” description for context [2][1].

question: What activities can I use to teach students about the replication crisis in a single 90-minute session?
answer:
You can run a focused 90‑minute session by combining two short, hands‑on activities from the Student’s Guide to Open Science with a ready‑made lesson plan that already targets the replication crisis [1][2].

**1. Start with a “Seat of a Replicator” activity (≈30 min).**  
Give each small group a recent psychology article and ask them to work through the checklist in Box 1 of the guide: identify the study’s aim, main hypotheses, design, measurement details, and data‑screening procedures [1]. This quick audit makes the replication problem concrete and highlights why many published studies are hard to reproduce.

**2. Follow with a preregistration exercise (≈30 min).**  
Using the notes from the first activity, have students draft a preregistration on a free repository (e.g., AsPredicted.org or the Open Science Framework) by filling in a template provided in Box 2 of the guide [1]. The exercise shows how open‑science tools can prevent the very issues they just uncovered.

**3. Wrap up with a structured lesson‑plan activity (≈20–30 min).**  
The “Understanding the replication crisis with app activities” lesson plan is already packaged for a single class session and includes an interactive app, discussion prompts, and a short debrief [2]. You can download it directly from the OSF link [Understanding the replication crisis with app activities](https://osf.io/cwaqj/).

*Optional add‑on:* If you have extra time, the “Registered Replication Report” lesson plan offers a concise walkthrough of how registered reports address replication problems [2] (download [Registered Replication Report](https://osf.io/2znr4/)).

question: How can I assess whether my students really understand p-values and statistical power?
answer:

**1. Use a simulation app that makes power and precision visible**  
Give students the free Shiny app that lets them vary sample size, effect size, and publication bias, then ask them to report how the p‑value distribution and power change. This directly tests their understanding of how statistical power and p‑values behave under different conditions. [1]  

**2. Have them explore a p‑hacking demonstration**  
Assign the FiveThirtyEight p‑hacking app, where students can manipulate analysis choices and see how p‑values can be driven below .05. Follow up with a short write‑up where they explain why the p‑values shift and what this means for scientific credibility. [1]

question: How should I supervise a master's thesis that is designed as a replication study?
answer:
Supervising a master’s thesis that is a replication study can be organized around the core recommendations of the FORRT handbook. Below is a step‑by‑step guide that follows the handbook’s advice and uses the provided resources.

### 1. Define the replication’s purpose and type  
* **Choose a clear aim** (e.g., test the original finding’s robustness, rule out a false‑positive, or extend the original design) and select the appropriate replication type (close/direct, close with extension, or conceptual) from Table 4.1 [1].  
* **Justify the target study** and the specific claims you will test [4].  

### 2. Conduct a reproduction first  
* **Attempt to reproduce the original results** before planning the new data collection. This can reveal coding errors, missing details, or robustness issues [1][4].  
* If the original code/data are unavailable, use automated tools such as **statcheck** or **papercheck** to verify reported statistics [1].  

### 3. Form the replication team  
* Involve graduate and undergraduate students at different levels, as the handbook recommends for “repetitive research” [1].  
* Assign clear roles (e.g., data manager, analyst, documentation lead) and ensure that all team members understand the replication’s scope.  

### 4. Pre‑registration and planning  
* **Pre‑register the study** (hypotheses, analysis plan, success criteria) using a Registered Report or an open pre‑registration platform [3].  
* **Determine sample size** using approaches suited to replications (small‑telescopes, equivalence testing, Bayesian design, or meta‑analytic estimates) rather than simply copying the original n [3].  

### 5. Document any deviations  
* When the original study lacks detail or when methodological improvements are needed, **record and justify every deviation** from the original protocol [3][4].

question: Does FORRT have a glossary of open science terms? Also, what is the difference between a preregistration and a registered report?
answer:
**Yes – FORRT maintains a public glossary of open‑science terms.**  
The glossary is hosted at [https://forrt.org/glossary/english/](https://forrt.org/glossary/english/) and contains more than 250 curated terms that were defined by over 110 collaborators during Phase 1 of the project [1]. Phase 2 is currently open for further improvements, extensions and translations [1].

**Difference between a preregistration and a registered report**

| Aspect | Preregistration | Registered Report |
|--------|----------------|--------------------|
| **Purpose** | Records, in advance, the hypotheses, analysis plan and success criteria for a study. It is mainly a transparency tool to guard against p‑hacking [2]. | Submits the study’s methods (including the preregistration) to peer review **before** data collection. If accepted, the journal commits to publishing the results regardless of the outcome [2]. |
| **Review** | Usually not peer‑reviewed; the document is posted on a registry. | Undergoes formal peer review; the methods are evaluated and the manuscript is provisionally accepted [2]. |
| **Effect on publication bias** | Reduces flexibility in analysis but does not guarantee publication. | Removes the “results‑driven” decision because acceptance is based on the planned methods, not on the findings [2]. |
| **Typical components** | Success criteria, analysis code, and (optionally) a manipulation check [2]. | Full preregistration plus a complete methods section that is reviewed and accepted in principle [2]. |

For more details on preregistration templates see the OSF links in the handbook, and a list of journals offering Registered Reports is available here: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1D4_k-8C_UENTRtbPzXfhjEyu3BfLxdOsn9j-otrO870/edit#gid=0) [2].

question: How to assign DOI to research data?
answer:
Assigning a DOI to your research data is most reliably done by depositing the data in a trusted, open‑access repository that automatically mints DOIs for deposited items.  

* **Choose a repository that issues DOIs** – the example in the Natural Sciences section shows that the underlying data for a paper were deposited in the RCSB Protein Data Bank and in Zenodo, both of which provide a DOI for the dataset [1].  
* **Upload your data with full metadata** – include a clear title, description, authors, funding information and a licence that permits reuse. Repositories such as Zenodo generate the DOI at the moment the record is made public [1].  
* **Link the DOI to your publication** – once the DOI is created, cite it in the reference list of your article and, if you publish in a venue that supports data citations (e.g., Wellcome Open Research), the DOI will be indexed alongside the paper [1].  
* **Make the data FAIR** – you can browse FAIR‑sharing registries for discipline‑specific repositories and standards to ensure your data are Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable (FAIR) [1].
